children: Nvidia's interim chief executive will have big questions to answer on Tuesday's earnings call with investors.

On Tuesday, the chip company is expected to report revenue and profit growth for the third quarter, with some analysts anticipating higher projections for the fourth quarter and full year. While the report might provide some relief to beaten-down shares, investors are far more focused on existential questions about the future of Nvidia's dominance without Jensen Huang.
"Interim CEO Colette Kress can vouch for the near term, but the leadership questions will outlast the call," StoneX analyst Cody Acree said in a note.

Nvidia shares have shed 10% of their value over the past five trading days following news that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. He subsequently stepped down from his role as chief executive.
A strong quarterly report and steady messaging could allow for a rally, as investors are trying to figure out where the stock will bottom out, Acree said.

For the third quarter, analysts polled by FactSet expect Nvidia to report revenue of $108.96 billion, up from $57.01 billion a year ago. Adjusted earnings are projected to be $2.48 a share, up from $1.29 a share.

Even if Nvidia hits its marks, it will be difficult for executives to completely dispel uncertainty about the future of the company. Huang is seen as one of the most important strategic leaders of the artificial-intelligence and semiconductor industry. Given that status, he was estimated to be worth roughly $1 trillion of Nvidia's valuation, according to Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives.

Many on Wall Street are worried that new leadership will slow down Nvidia's break-neck pace of rolling out new products. Questions about how the company will be run under a new leader won't be fully answered until a permanent successor is appointed.

There is also some uncertainty about whether Huang will be brought back, although Ives and other analysts have said that is an unlikely outcome. When President Trump was asked Monday what he would think about Huang returning as chief executive, he said, "That certainly isn't a bad idea."

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has taken an opposing stance, saying Nvidia needs to shake up its board and go outside the company to find its next chief executive. He is also asking for Nvidia board members to answer questions about working with shell companies, many of which are in Singapore.

That points to another concern among investors: that espionage allegations could bring greater scrutiny to the company. More surveillance over trade with China could lead to fewer sales in certain geographies, including Singapore and Malaysia, UBS analysts Timothy Arcuri and Seth Cho said in a note. In a worst case for Nvidia, revenue could be dented by as much as 10%, the analysts said.

While questions remain, Nvidia still stands as an industry leader at a time when demand from AI hyperscalers is almost unlimited. A strong quarterly report could help the stock get back on track after weeks of bad news, Ives said.
"A clean quarter and guide from the tech stalwart would be an important step forward after this black cloud week," he said.
